Losing the faint signatures of high-frequency gravitational waves (HF-GWs) represents a pivotal bottleneck in gravitational wave (GW) observatories. In this study, we assess the potential of Sloshing-Sagnac interferometers (SSIs) to enhance sensitivity across the HF-GW spectrum. Our analysis reveals that integrating an SSI into a main detector's configuration could boost high-frequency sensitivity by up to an order of magnitude. We also explore the optimization of this performance and provide a detailed forecast for the next-generation Einstein Telescope regarding HF-GWs detectability.

Dynamic time-division duplexing (TDD) allows each base station to schedule uplink and downlink transmission modes independently according to its own traffic load. Unfortunately, this decentralization leads to intercell cross-interference, making the combined problem of power distribution and resource allocation a mixed-integer non-convex challenge that is NP-hard. To address this, we introduce a computationally efficient, decentralized framework that decouples the scheduling and power control processes. The proposed method first distributes power across cells in a decentralized manner and subsequently assigns transmission modes using a non-cooperative game to reach a mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium. Two different payoff calculation methods within the game model explore the impact of cross-interference representations and the associated communication overhead. Simulation studies in an outdoor, high-density small-scale cellular environment demonstrate that these proposed strategies significantly surpass the performance of static TDD systems.

This process ensures that untrustworthy instances do not negatively impact model performance. Our experiments using a half-million-class Image dataset demonstrate that this approach effectively identifies untrustworthy inputs, quantifies their proportion, and improves overall model performance with minimal human intervention.

This study concentrates on two pivotal aspects of cross-domain text-to-SQL semantic parsing, namely schema linkage and value instantiation. Furthermore, we develop two distinct value-injection approaches that bridge the gap between current zero-shot semantic parsers—often neglecting actual database content—and complex operations requiring executed values. These strategies leverage trained row features from the column selection task to inform both trained and newly encountered domains. Extensive experiments conducted across multiple database benchmarks validate the effectiveness of proposed methods in empowering models to handle previously unseen database environments without task-specific demonstrations.

This paper investigates the deployment of differential privacy (DP) within graph-structured environments. It examines various DP formulations applicable both to publishing data and associated statistics, and to conducting machine learning on graph-based information, specifically focusing on graph neural networks (GNNs). Furthermore, this paper explores the interplay DP plays with de-anonymization attacks and other privacy threats, highlighting current research gaps, unresolved questions, and promising future directions.

Full waveform inversion (FWI) serves as the most effective strategy for enhancing seismic imaging resolution and exploring the subsurface geology. However, the severe nonlinearity of the update mechanisms in FWI typically restricts these models to function within a shallow layer above an initially accurate image. We contend that expanding the field of views of FWI—specifically by incorporating time-domain information and incorporating sources that represent extended spatial areas—brings significant advantages. Our contribution includes developing novel techniques that implement our proposed time-domain and extended-domain methodologies. The effectiveness of these refined approaches is substantiated by experimental outcomes that compare them favorably against current wavefront inversion technologies.

This study presents our novel introduction of the asymmetric noisy voter model, which examines how joint migration and competition determine the dynamics of spatial populations. Within this framework, a unidirectional migration occurs between adjacent patches, where invaders replace a portion of the local residents' genetic material. Competition intensity is modulated by the energy required to survive in new versus established patches: high-energy movers are negatively selected, as successful invasion requires a patches of lower cost; conversely, low-energy travelers thrive due to their efficiency. This system establishes a competition-colonization tradeoff, creating multiple stable states where only limited pairs of invaders can stably coexist based on the sum of their costs. However, noise-specific migration creates instability that disrupts this balance; even migrants with combined costs below the threshold face total exclusion. Our analysis reveals a critical noise threshold, where crossing it causes the disappearance of the domain of attraction for the invasive species, effectively erasing them from the system and demonstrating how noise-driven exclusion overturns deterministic competitive outcomes.

Driven by an exceptional rise in the need for remote work, the push to automate and manage experiments from a distance has become increasingly important. This project details the technical implementation of a two-dimensional (2D) Laser Doppler Vibrometry (LDV) measurement obtained by remotely controlling Single-Point LDV hardware. The goal of this study is to enable engineers to operate the LDV equipment and store data directly from the system for practical applications. To achieve this, the project utilizes the LDV system and accompanying software provided by Polytec GmbH, enhanced with the LDV ToolKit (LDT) for single-point configurations. The solution involves replacing the original automated scanning motor controls with a remotely operated interface. Instead, the operator manually maneuvers the LDV probe using a joystick to manually track a target within the test area. The integrated software captures images of the object, overlays the specific measurement point, and facilitates real-time monitoring of the frequencies required for each point. Upon completion of an object scan, the system automatically generates and saves the resulting 2D heat map data.

Although current developments in programmable electrostatic phase plates spark doubts about their utility for certain applications, this study examines various plate designs aimed specifically at rectifying spherical aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Our findings indicate that while spherical aberration compensation by these programs introduces some inherent limitations, it is indeed feasible to achieve sub-1-angstrom imaging widths.

We offer a qualitative evaluation of potentially problematic outputs from contextualized embedding methods used to identify historical semantic shifts. We introduce an ensemble technique, which surpasses prior contextualized strategies, serving as the foundation for a deep dive into predicted levels of semantic change for English vocabulary across fifty years. Results indicate that these contextualized methods frequently generate high change scores even when no actual diachronic semantic shift occurs, a phenomenon likely stemming from the lack of explicit timing information in these models and their tendency to use high-dimensional, sparse representations sensitive to local context variations. We argue that research communities utilizing these contextualized embeddings for semantic change detection should adopt a more cautious stance due to inflated and spurious positive results, ultimately calling for a better theoretical understanding of how they capture or fail to capture semantic stability or change.

Interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM), characterized by nuclei shifting oscillatory movements perpendicular to the retinal plane during neuroepithelial expansion, serves as a reliable biomarker for neural retina development defects and a key focus in developmental neuroscience research. While the precise mechanisms regulating this movement remain unclear, it is hypothesized that a diffusive model could explain these dynamics. In this study, we tested this hypothesis specifically within the IKNM of embryonic zebrafish retinas. Our results offer strong support for the validity of the diffusion model. Specifically, we observed a linear correlation between the mean displacement of migrating nuclei and time, and we found the standard displacement of these nuclei conformed to expected increases. Additionally, the frequency of these nuclear movements aligned with the time constant predicted by diffusion principles. Finally, our experiments demonstrated that altering the diffusivity of IKNM markers affects both the standard and oscillatory standard displacements of migrating nuclei accordingly. Given these findings, we conclude that the standard displacement serves as an appropriate indicator for evaluating deviations in nuclear movement under various pathological or physiological conditions, suggesting this work holds significant practical value for clinical and experimental applications.

Parabolic brush theory provides an effective framework for analyzing equilibrium configurations of molten polymers on curved interfaces, although it inherently excludes the physical presence of end exclusion zones. The research highlights how this "end-included" model accurately captures surface-tension-like forces, surface-stress-like effects, and the specific mechanics governing the formation and behavior of end-exclusion zones. The magnitude of these effects fluctuates based on the meticulous arrangement of polymer chain ends and is significantly influenced by geometric curvature. The available mathematical tools and the incorporated physical constraints offer a robust basis for investigating the fundamental characteristics of strongly stretched, amphi-paetic polymer systems confined to complex, three-dimensional curved interfacial structures.

In 2001, V. Levenshtein introduced the sequence reconstruction problem, a theoretical framework with significant practical applications in genetics. Within this model, a unknown but fixed source sequence is assumed to exist; furthermore, various machines operate by reading this sequence and introducing specific types of errors. If a sequence of size $N$ is produced, determining the original source sequence becomes feasible provided $N$ is sufficiently large, given that the Reconstruction Number (RN) for any sequence $S$ represents the minimum number of machines required for its identification. When the allowed operations limit the Hamming distance between strings, this problem shifts into a metric reconstruction number (MRN) context. Our study investigates the MRNs across several string configurations, including binary strings, permutations, specific families such as Birkhoff's permutation matrices and Levi's symmetric distribution numbers, offering new results and computations for each group.

Accurately and swiftly predicting river flow velocities is critical for various applications, such as managing flood risks. Although recent research has deployed deep learning models to forecast hydrodynamic variables, these methods often require extensive training data, which may be limited for specific rivers, rendering broad generalization uncertain. Alternatively, the Shallow Water Equations (SWE), supported by robust numerical schemes, can provide reliable flow velocity predictions without extensive generalization concerns but remain computationally demanding for real-time use. To resolve this tension, we developed a rapid SWE inference model based on an unsupervised deep neural network. By leveraging the SWE operator as a prior, the network converges to a solution with minimal input, enabling real-time velocity predictions. We validated this approach against a dataset containing one hour of continuous camera footage and corresponding Eulerian water flow measurements collected during a major flood event; the results confirmed the model's accuracy in matching actual flow velocities.

High-dynamic-range (HDR) imaging is achieved by merging a set of exposures taken at varying levels, allowing devices like smartphones with limited internal dynamic ranges to capture full brightness and contrast. This study proposes a technique to automatically determine exposure parameters using a camera characteristic function. Additionally, it defines a novel merging approach relying on weighted averaging through an optimization framework. These strategies have been deployed as an HDR application for mobile use, proving their practical application. Comparative analyses against existing benchmarks confirm the method's efficiency and computational effectiveness.

Causal deep learning represents a significant and rapidly advancing intersection of machine learning and statistics, equipping deep learning models with statistical tools to build robust, transferable systems grounded in causal structures. This review offers a structured deep-learning-focused survey of the causal deep learning literature, organizing over 150 recent publications by architecture, modality, and application area to facilitate research entry. Beyond a comprehensive review of current architectures for supervised and unsupervised causal representation learning, classification, regression, and generative tasks, the work provides detailed analyses of integrable causal identifiability results, classifications based applied domains and data types, and emerging trends. We also navigate emerging architectural innovations across multimodal causal architectures, video and audio-visual systems, causal graphs and networks, recurrent and transformer models, multi-agent and communicative agent systems, and scalable infrastructures for millions of agents interacting causally. Finally, we examine open research challenges in causal deep learning, including architecture design considerations, generative models, sample efficiency, reliability across tasks and domains, theory for complex causal architectures, and emerging modalities such as causal large language models and natural language processing.

This note introduces and analyzes a new class of maps known as oriented colored broken submersions. It represents the most fundamental class of maps complying with an h-principle (here referred to as b-principle); in two dimensions, it approximates oriented submersions notably by ensuring every oriented colored broken submersion from a 2-manifold to a closed, simply connected manifold is boardant to a submersion. Additionally, we demonstrate that the Madsen-Weiss theorem (the well-known Mumford Conjecture), fits effectively this overarching b-principle framework. Given an h-version of the principle applicable to these maps alongside Harer stability and Miller Morita results, a derivation of the Madsen-Weiss (Munford) theorem becomes viable.

This study presents a performance evaluation comparing Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) preconditioners for cardiac mechanical simulations on both structured and unstructured finite element meshes. Since myocardial mechanical behavior follows three-dimensional finite elasticity equations—which are discretized spatially to form a massive nonlinear algebraic system solved via the Newton-Krylov method—this framework relies on BDDC and AMG acceleration techniques to resolve the associated Jacobian systems. A thorough analysis of critical BDDC settings is provided, establishing a robust framework for assessing computational performance. Results from this evaluation on a detailed finite model of three-dimensional left ventricular mechanics highlight key distinctions in the efficacy of these scalable solver options.

Consequently, this study analyzes the diffusion of fractional (long-time memory-corrupted) particles under conditions of spatially varying diffusivity. utilizing the 1D time-space fractional advection-dispersion equation, we examine a diffusivity structure linked to local superdiffusive dynamics; in this framework, the diffusivity’s temporal dependence at constant position aligns precisely with that observed in the classic, uncorrelated diffusive process at diffusion distances of similar scale. Despite producing specific non-Gaussian diffusive outcomes with distinct spatial temporal diffusivity scaling laws that compete with the study of both sub- and superdiffusive scenarios (the latter including independent log-normal distributions), these methods ultimately converge to Gaussian results if diffusivity correlations are limited or the timespan is short. This study introduces a deep learning framework that utilizes Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to recover high-resolution turbulent velocity fields from very low-resolution data across various Reynolds numbers. The Multiscale Enhanced Super-Resolution GAN (MS-ESRGAN) serves as the model for reconstruction and is assessed using direct numerical simulation (DNS) of turbulent channel flows with large longitudinal ribs tested at multiple Reynolds numbers. The findings indicate the model's capability to accurately generate high-resolution velocity fields, encompassing both field properties and turbulent statistics, from inputs derived from two distinct low-resolution resolutions. Furthermore, the results demonstrate the model's potential for supergeneralization by reconstructing velocity fields at Reynolds levels different from those used during training, without additional instruction or adaptation for those specific cases.

Although significant advancements have been made in applying reinforcement learning to robotics, gaming, and other demanding areas, considerable obstacles persist when deploying these algorithms in critical, evolving open-world settings. A primary issue remains the tendency of reinforcement learning models to generalize poorly to new tasks lying outside their training data distributions. Consequently, a pressing opportunity exists for developing robust metrics to quantify 'memories' retained from past experiences and to assess MEMORy capabilities—specifically, an environment where agents acquire skills over time and a associated benchmark for evaluating lifelong learning strategies. We present L2OpenWorld, comprising a constructed world and new metrics to measure an agent's ability to recall and utilize this information. Our metrics assess how effectively a model can leverage these memories against indices testing various forms of forgetting, such as catastrophic interference, reverse forgetting, and the retention of distinct competencies. Experiments utilizing standard reinforcement learning approaches reveal that current agents typically exhibit limited long-term memory, struggling to keep old skills intact despite the capability to execute them previously.

Process discovery, estimation, and analysis are critical for the effective operation of enterprise systems. However, existing techniques frequently neglect process improvement initiatives or struggle to handle complex patterns like sporadic executive support activities and screen-sharing collaborations. To address these issues, screen-based process analysis (SPA) was introduced; while effective, it remains limited to discovered processes within a specific system. Building upon SPA as a foundation, we propose the Stream-based Process Analysis (SPA) framework to enable both the discovery and improvement of processes across any endeavor. This approach synthesizes various information sources—including screen-based data—with real-time event logs and monitoring strategies that target process bottlenecks. By leveraging these diverse inputs, stream-based process analysis (SPA) facilitates more informed analysis and inherently captures behaviors such as screen-shared tasks that might otherwise go unrecordored in traditional event logs. Furthermore, this work introduces an innovative processing enhancement methodology designed to complement stream-based discovery (SPA). The approach utilizes a risk-sensitive algorithm to identify process improvement opportunities by closely examining screen-based process logs alongside either event logs or monitoring data in real time. Once a region for enhancement is identified using screen-based discovery (SPA), the system employs a detailed analysis via monitoring to pinpoint exact process deviations. This combined method ensures a more accurate identification of process improvement needs, particularly those characterized as "rare" based on their appearance in screen-based process logs but verified through monitoring. To conclude, we illustrate how screen-based process logs, when integrated with other data types, can identify improvement opportunities

This research explores cross-lingual sentiment analysis for Croatian news through zero- and few-shot learning approaches. The study focuses on categorizing Croatian news into positive, negative, and neutral classes by leveraging the Slovene dataset. The methodology employs an architecture built on a trilingual BERT model trained on English, Slovene, and Croatian texts. The paper examines various configurations using bilingual datasets, introducing introduction of unrelated languages into training, as well as testing different model training strategies, including multiskemalML for sentiment analysis. The study includes both few-shot and zero-shot setups; the latter achieves novel results for opinion mining in Croatian via leveraging skills from Slovene sources.

X-ray imaging serves as an accessible and affordable diagnostic tool for evaluating pulmonary conditions in COVID-19 patients. Nevertheless, the widespread implementation of such systems relies heavily on collecting extensive, geographically diverse clinical datasets to effectively address variations in disease progression and severity among infected individuals. This study presents an innovative framework leveraging geocoding and linguistics-based coding to extract spatial characteristics directly from images of COVID-19 patients upon their hospitalization in ICU settings. This method integrates location metadata and descriptive information from disparate datasets, converting textual attributes into unified numerical vectors through coding. Leveraging this proposed design, we analyzed over 100,000 images sourced from greater than a million entries across multiple distinct datasets. Following the evaluation of various deep learning architectures, we determined that a ResNet5 model trained with geocoding and linguistically coded features demonstrated superior accuracy, specifically achieving an F1 score of 0.9333 for accurately classifying currently admitted ICU COVID-19 cases. Additionally, we conducted thorough analyses on identified potential locational and pictorial indicators, subsequently introducing a novel dataset encompassing more than 100,000 images, 200,000 coordinates, and 20 million linguistic codes to facilitate subsequent diverse investigations into related infectious disease topics.

This paper examines the reasons behind the high false positive rate in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) and examines the limited impact of existing methods to mitigate them. We propose a method that improves the Recall@k of relationship detection by a margin of +5.7 percentage points (a relative 10% increase) over the baseline. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/yourname/yourrepo.

This study utilizes detailed observations of a specific galaxy group containing a central, massive object at approximately 250 kparsecs away. The research focuses on a target that exhibits significant asymmetry, a high concentration of stellar material, a high stellar velocity dispersion, and a supermassive black hole, all of which distinguish it as a quasi-typical type. The authors present detailed analyses of velocity dispersions, rotational curves, and asymmetric structures alongside the results of theoretical imaging simulations regarding kinematical data. The research aims to address several critical questions: the trustworthiness of rotational curves derived from highly asymmetric systems; the origin of high velocity dispersion and star formation activity in central regions; and whether these traits classify the object as a nascent bulge or a unique low-mass early-type galaxy. The findings reveal that this isolated, massive black hole system exhibits characteristics of both disordered motions and asymmetries congruent with those usually observed in elliptical and bulged galaxies. However, it lacks the classic classical morphological features typically associated with such classifications. The research suggests bulge formation has occurred within a distorted, inclined disk through a star formation burst triggered by black hole-driven outflows that cleared out the interstellar gas. Despite this developing bulge, the surrounding low inclination remains unclassified as an elliptical galaxy due the persistence of the external asymmetric mass. The study concludes with insights regarding the connection among morphological transformations, outflows, and energy input from massive black holes.

Based on our data analysis, solenons derived from solar neural decay provide high velocities,接近 or exceeding the speed of light ($\gtrsim 0.5c$). These particles traverse distances of approximately 145,000 kilometers (~0.4 astronomical units) before decaying into electrons and solenons. Our study suggests that standard neutron monitor stations should be able to detect such events, highlighting a mechanism by which significant particle floods reach Earth following moderate solar system flares.

This study examines the extended luminosity excess observed in the globular cluster NGTS-3, previously noted by Li et al. (2023). While Li et al. linked this brightness to a massive planet undergoing tidal disruption on the stellar surface, our analysis suggests an alternative: the brightening likely results from the consumption of a planetary core composed of light elements occurring just above the stellar convective zone. Furthermore, we question the inference made by Li et al. that angular momentum interaction between the engulfed object and the star is necessary to explain the system's rotation; rather, the surface spinning of HD 31648 may be primordial, established prior to the diving incident. Furthermore, the core's migration into the stellar interior appears to account for the measured deepening of the convective zone and the simultaneous preservation of high effective temperature and stellar radius.

Rapidly circulating through social media channels, fake news poses significant threats to public safety and security. Traditional detection frameworks often fail to accurately identify emerging fraudulent content, a vulnerability exacerbated by data silos and the explosion of new platforms. Addressing this challenge, we introduce an approach designed to discover emergent misinformation by leveraging cross-source knowledge; this method first learns a unified graph-structured representation for content and metadata to facilitate the sharing of patterns, then employs neural meta-process networks to identify fake content. This creates a modality-fusion detection pipeline capable of adapting quickly to new domains using only a minimal amount of seed data. To validate the strategy, we assessed it across three large, diverse real-world datasets. Results demonstrate a significant improvement in the accurate discovery of fake content compared to prior methods, particularly when generalizing to datasets outside those during training.

Recently, research into multidimensional Golay complementary arrays (GCA) has been fueled by their promise in omnidirectional precoding for the newly generalized form of Golay complementary matrices (GCM). This study establishes new construction methods for GCA quads and GCA pairs with the help of defined identities across commutative rings, generalizing the concept of GCM. Specifically, we prove the validity of quaternary GCA quandles in a high-dimensional array size product that meets certain auxiliary diversity requirements. Although we conjecture that there is no bound on binary GCM quadrups of arbitrary and widely-diverged dimensions which we confirmed in a non-independent proof. We also explore bounds on quaternary GCM quadrups for instances where one dimension lacks proportionality in terms of two odd numbers. Finally some test results are evaluated to show that our proposed construction methods achieve significant performance improvements over existing designs.

Quantum tunneling, a non-classical phenomenon where a particle crosses a barrier it classically couldn't surmount, finds a macroscopic analog in silicon through electron motion between two equivalent \{113\} nanometer-scale divot defects. This process generates oscillations in the nuclear magnetic resonance signals of phosphorus donor atoms, an effect harnessed in early high-sensitivity field sensors and silicon-based two-photon qubits. Now, we utilize ultra-narrow Gaussian-shaped donor atom clusters to investigate these tunneling behaviors, focusing on how varying their lateral separation alters oscillation frequencies and reveals previously unseen patterns. This method also enables precise 3D nuclear magnetic sensing with heightened precision and resolution. Furthermore, we have realized a two-level silicon-based "clock" state, leveraging this capability to perform precise two-nucleus magnetic imaging, which is essential for developing scalable silicon nuclear magnetic quantum computers.

Complex systems, ranging from biological networks to macroeconomic systems and social structures, are characterized by their intricate interconnections. Representing these as graphs enables the application of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), a class of machine learning algorithms that has proven effective across various domains. This article provides a comprehensive overview of recent advancements in using GNNs to analyze dynamic systems and evolve with them. We begin with a formal introduction to core GNN mechanisms and architectural designs. Subsequently, we explore the analysis of dynamic system dynamics and architectural evolution. We also address the critical challenge of scalability and present our contributions to the development of causal and generative models focused on dynamic systems. Concluding with a summary of our work using these tools to investigate real-world complex networks, including the Human Brain and climate systems such as the Atmosphere and Ocean.

Laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) represents a new minimally invasive approach for ablating intracranial structures, serving effectively as a neuromodulation strategy to manage disorders arising from abnormal brain activity. Nevertheless, the invasive nature of the procedure, along the need to master precise needle navigation within the skull, mandates the development of robust prediction and monitoring techniques. Since implementing intraoperative LiDAR and CT fusion techniques remains technically demanding and costly, the paper proposes a novel method that leverages a lesion synthesis ground truth to identify deviations between measured and anticipated free-space conditions during operations. The proposed pipeline begins with the segmentation of thermal images acquired during LITT interventions to act as synthesis training labels. These images are then employed in an end-to-end training framework to instruct a deep learning model capable of detecting and synthesizing brain lesions upon receiving standard pre-operative and peri-operative data. The model under consideration is an improvement over a basic GAN, utilizing the superior reconstruction capabilities of a Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE). This enhanced architecture was validated on a training cohort of 31 subjects, demonstrating high performance on an independent test set comprising 11 patients, with a reported mean lesion synthesis accuracy of 0.93 ± 0.07.

Feature extraction offers a viable strategy to mitigate dimensionality challenges within high-dimensional datasets. As a prevalent self-supervised learning technique, contrastive learning has recently attracted substantial attention. In this research, we introduced a unified framework grounded in a novel interpretation of contrastive learning, applicable to both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework first establishes an initial representation space through contrastive learning and subsequently refines these representations either via clustering (in unsupervised cases) or classification tasks (in supervised cases). Notably, the proposed supervised approach achieves state-of-the-art performance across five distinct text datasets, while the unsupervised method yields significant improvements in high-stakes real-world applications, including cancer sub-type classification and COVID-19 risk assessment.

We present novel constructions of infinite families of locally arc transitive graphs where each graph possesses exactly two vertex orbits, the automorphism group restricted to one orbit acts as a quasi-primitive group of the "star normal quotient twisted wreath" type. Model selection or sparse modelling for categorical variables remains problematic, even with a moderate variable count, as encoding each category requires a parameter, quickly leading to non-solutions. Although Group Lasso is an established and efficient tool for selecting continuous or categorical variables, its estimates for individual levels of selected factors are rarely identical. Because of this, standard Group Lasso fails to produce sparse solutions, which is critical: a factor should be modeled only if all its levels share the same effect. We propose a single, straight-forward modification to Group Lasso that enforces equality of coefficients within chosen factor levels, ensuring a sparse structure, improved interpretability, and more stable predictions.

Although Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit human-like capabilities across a wide range of areas, they face severe issues when dealing with novel domains, a challenge known as Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) skill. To address this, we developed an innovative framework called Structured Knowledge Infusion for LLMs (SKILL). Our approach begins with a baseline variant of the prompt engineering technique known as PCT. Building on this foundation, SKILL enhances performance in scenarios where essential background information for solving tasks is missing, resulting in more robust solutions compared to baseline methods. Our experiments demonstrate that using PCT leads to significant improvements across all five evaluated LLM variants due to the approach's efficiency, while the SKILL enhancement yields an average 3.3 percentage point increase, showcasing the value of integrating domain-specific knowledge.

Spatial anti-aliasing is critical for both the visual quality and rendering performance of line joins where road segments intersect on vector maps. Given OpenGL's limitations, a standard approach involves splicing multiple triangles to approximate fan-shaped or rounded connections; however, this method often produces suboptimal aesthetic results. To address issues like blurriness and shape inconsistencies that arise from simple alternatives such as square or linear joins, we introduce a dynamic, OpenGL-based rendering technique using a "tangent join." This solution computes the exact control points for Tjoins within an orthogonally projected equidistant map projection, rendering three quadratically Bezier-curved sectors that smoothly merge at angles. We evaluated this approach on a dataset covering 66,000 kilometers of road networks in Shanghai, demonstrating its clear advantages over existing methods. Additionally, performance tests indicate that the proposed technique significantly outperforms standard approaches, achieving a 23% higher frames per second (FPS) average and a 3.17-fold increase in frames per second variance stability.

Recent initiatives aim to enhance the representation of convective clouds within coarse-resolution global models through a Multiple Fluid Framework (MFF). This approach replaces traditional simplified parameterizations with an internal dynamics model governed by an MFF that incorporates an equation of state and essential physical processes specific to the target phenomenon under consideration. However, developing an MFF internal model based on current global model capabilities presents a major hurdle. This study takes an initial step toward that goal by formulating a vertical single-column model (SCM) Rayleigh-Bénard convection (RBC) system using a two-fluid framework (treating air and thermally lighter buoyant elements as distinct fluids). Although simpler than the multiple fluids involved in real-shallow convective boundary layers, this two-fluid non-Boussinesque model effectively reproduces key statistics from established Boussinesque RBC large-eddy simulations (LES) and theoretical predictions regarding heat, momentum, light buoyancy, and condensed heavy buoyancy. This model explicitly accounts for the generation, distribution, and deactivation of buoyant elements, as well as the release of latent heat via non-Boussinesque phase-change. Its primary advantage lies in being more physically comprehensive than current one-fluid latent-heat-generation models, which often overlook the explicit dynamics of turbulent mixing. We argue that this two-fluid latent-heat single-column model offers a feasible pathway to advance the complex two-fluid dynamics required for future implementations in global multiple fluids systems.

We examine three independent Jaynes-Cummings systems involving atom pairs where correlations exist between some atoms while the third remains initially uncorrelated. Our investigation focuses on the criteria required for these three uncorrelated atoms to achieve genuine multipartite entanglement. We determine that creating genuine multipartite entanglement is unattainable if the interaction cavity of an initially uncorrelated atom shares only classical correlations with any other cavity. Furthermore, we observe that if the interaction cavity housing the uncorrelated atom is highly entangled with any other cavity, the resulting atomic states *can* exhibit genuine multipartite entanglement. This non-trivial finding offers a potential strategy for generating multipartite-entangled atoms through Jaynes-Cummings interactions.

Emotional monitoring through public opinion on social media platforms has garnered significant attention within the corporate realm for its utility in gaugating public sentiment toward various entities, such as startup ventures, established brands, and even political figures. In response, I have engineered a novel LSTM-based algorithm tailored to assess emotional tone within Twitter streams. This model, when subjected to the Twitter Opinion Board dataset, outperformed most comparable methods in accuracy. Furthermore, I investigated several key aspects of the algorithm, encompassing the function of word embeddings within the LSTM architecture, the model's ability to capture semantic sentiment, and how varying amounts of training data influence performance outcomes.

Reconstructing quantum states in continuous-variable systems like the radiation field faces significant obstacles, primarily stemming from the intrinsic dimensionality and dimensionality-dependent intricacy of their Hilbert space. To circumvent these challenges, various strategies have been employed, including the utilization of displacement operators, the employment of Wigner function reconstruction, and the application of optimization techniques leveraging tomographic data. A distinguishing and valuable trait of Wigner functions is their direct visualization of pure-state entanglement and, more broadly, H. synchronization—a phenomenon emerging when a system's joint state fails to be expressed as the separation of individual component states into the uniqueness of the global state. This work presents an analytical derivation for the exact reconstruction of Wigner functions directly from experimental data, revealing how such reconstruction is impacted by the emergence of H. synchronization. Furthermore, using a model optical parametric amplifier (OPA) that yields entanglement and H. synchronization at varying levels of input intensity, we investigate the specific manifestations of these changes in the resulting tomographic images.

360-degree video streaming delivers immersive user experiences, though it depends heavily on extensive network bandwidth consuming. Effecting bandwidth savings can be managed through partial transmission, which requires precise data on user viewing regions, or "hotspots,"; however, predicting these areas remains a significant technological challenge. The current study introduces a novel approach that forecasts user gaze patterns using metadata from video descriptions and associated subtitles. Machine learning techniques drive this non-deep solution, leveraging feature extraction from subtitle sequences to anticipate potential attention centers. Tests, assessed via diverse evaluation benchmarks, demonstrate that this subtitle-based strategy outperforms existing techniques, particularly those relying on history-independent user behavior, especially in predicting hotspots for 360-degree virtual tourism content.

"Matrix product operator methods are commonly employed to simulate both equilibrium and out-of-equilibrium systems, provided that the time evolution scale or inverse temperature allows for a sufficiently low bond dimension. However, these techniques have lacked strict mathematical backing because previous approximations for time evolution and thermal states necessitated a bond dimension that escalates with system volume. To resolve this limitation, we propose PEPOs capable of approximating the Heisenberg time evolution of local operators alongside their thermal expectation values independently of the system's size, with the bond dimension dependent solely on temperature or time. We furthermore demonstrate the application of this framework in estimating expectation values for quenched dynamics and thermal correlation functions.

This research examines the decoupling theory for a wide range of $C^5$ surfaces $\mathbb{M}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ that do not possess planar locations of zero Gaussian curvature, encompassing cases beyond graphs of mixed homogeneous polynomials. Analyzing $\mathbb{M}$ facilitates refracting standard linear iterative decoupling into more general frameworks. The methodology synthesizes Taylor-based expansions with partial differential equation-based propagation to address surfaces varied from those with special algebraic properties to others lacking flat points of zero Hessian. The outcome establishes the validity of decoupling for all such surfaces, demonstrating their common structural similarity despite not being proven to share every specific property.

The paper estimates the uncertainties associated with infrared renormalons in the (color dipole) gluon distribution, demonstrating that non-linear saturation effects at small $x$ give rise to a double pole in the infrared region. This distinct feature contrasts with the single infrared pole produced by the standard, widely accepted small-$x$ BFKL distribution. Consequently, standard TMD PDF calculations at leading order—typically derived from the Yennie-Furmanishak (though not explicitly specified, likely refers to standard factorization) or similar frameworks—suffer from significantly enhanced infrared renormalon issues compared to conventional treatments.

Nanometer-thick rare-earth-transition metal (RE-TM) alloys, characterized by their exceptionally strong and tunable magnetic properties, have established themselves as a cornerstone within the field of magnetophotonics. Although researchers have extensively investigated how ellipticity and incidence angle influence a material's surface crystal response to light polarization, the impact of propagation direction remains largely unexplored. In this study, we identified a bidirectional asymmetric mirror system in the near-infrared spectrum that arises from pairing a cubic Gd film with (111)-oriented Tb/Tm surfaces. This surface crystal exhibits directional asymmetry along a linear path: circularly polarized lights traveling in opposite directions experience distinct reflective behaviors dictated by the material's circular magnetic dichroism. Specifically, switching the propagation direction of linearly polarized light instantly switches the reflected output between two orthogonally polarized circular states by switching the illumination from right-handed to left-handed circular polarization. Notably, this directional-asymmetric mirage effect survives even when the surface is covered in moisture or organic contaminants that create a mid-film barrier. Functioning as a non-reciprocal crystal optical element without the requirement for an external magnetic field, this discovery offers a promising pathway for developing all-optical magnetic memory storage and bidirectional communication systems that possess high density, efficiency, and resilience.

Knowledge distillation serves as a proven strategy for expediting deep neural networks, where well-established theories support transferring capabilities from large white-box models to smaller counterparts with comparable accuracy. However, these approaches rarely address the critical challenge of distilling data from black-box systems, which are prevalent in industry but lack open architecture access. Furthermore, most existing methods rely on carefully designed student models; in contrast, this study examines a more realistic scenario involving completely free-standing student models. We introduce DKB, Decision-based Knowledge Bridging, an efficient algorithm capable of extracting information from such closed systems. To broaden the model's applicability, we also develop an effective strategy to uncover meaningful details embedded in the probabilistic output distributions of black-box targets. We further extend DBC by integrating a transfer learning-based component to capture additional bridgable knowledge from the same systems. Extensive testing, including large-scale experiments using a publicly available white ghost image classifier, effectively validates our methodology. As a further exploration, we investigate the link between DBC and zero-shot distillation, demonstrating its capacity to transfer effective information across unrelated architectures with no direct white-box training. To support this research, we also release all trained white-box image models and corresponding training data, including image captions, as a public dataset.

This report presents the first observation of the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode alongside evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} S^0 K$ process. These findings are based on a data sample of 1.0 $\times$ 10 $^{0}$ pb$^{-1}$ collected by the LHCb experiment at $\sqrt{s}=7$ and $8$ teV. The measured branching fractions are $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 S^0 K) = \dots$ and $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0 S} ) = \dots$ respectively, with both values normalized to $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to X^0 S^0 C^0) = \dots$. The corresponding significances are $5.9\sigma$ for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 S^0 K$ decay and $3.0\sigma$ for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0 S} $ decay.

Constructing the submodule lattice $L(M)$ for an arbitrary module $M$ is inherently challenging, particularly when the module lacks a multiplicity-free structure. For any given module $M$, there exists some auxiliary module $M'$ containing $L(M)$ as a substructure, where $M'$ can be explicitly realized through a set of submodules of $M$. Although $L(M)$ is not guaranteed to be the most faithful representation within $M'$, it provides a viable alternative. Our approach computatively builds $L(M)$ from these super-factors: starting with an arbitrary $M'$, we identify and remove every "unfeasible" submodule that does not correspond to a valid factor in $M$. Our findings demonstrate that this procedure is substantially more streamlined and efficient than the prevalent algorithm by Stibitz, which utilizes the complete collection of submodules of $M$. Moreover, for any $M$ with a prime characteristic $p$ where all factors have $p$-adic multiplicity one in $M'$, we established that $M'$ already houses the authentic, collapsed lattice structure of $M$.

Imitation learning primarily enhances reinforcement learning efficiency by utilizing expert demonstrations. However, in practical scenarios, obtaining such expert data is often unfeasible or prohibitively expensive. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a new framework dubbed Co-Imitation Learning (CoIL), designed to boost an agent's performance in a shared multi-agent environment without relying on external expert data. Within CoIL, learning agents improve individually by learning from one another's experiences. Although straightforward in concept, naive imitation strategies can yield detrimental outcomes, as an action effective for one agent might negatively impact others or the collective system performance. Consequently, an agent adopting another's policy must evaluate both the adopter's potential gain and the overall effect on shared objectives. To capture this nuance, we propose a new metric, called Differential Imitation Reward (D-IMR), which evaluates the balance between individual benefits and collective consequences. Furthermore, we develop a value-based algorithm grounded in the D-IMR that enables structured knowledge transfer. Our experimental results, conducted across three distinct tasks, demonstrate that Co-IL effectively utilizes peer knowledge to achieve higher performance than standard baseline approaches.

This paper proposes an enhanced algorithm to compute the distance between a specific integer and a valid Hamming-weight-constrained value, utilizing it to derive superior methods for calculating the free distance of convolutional codes and the distance properties of block codes. Convergence toward the exact numerical result is achieved by restricting the search space; as sample sizes grow larger, the algorithm functions as a rigorous Monte Carlo method. We also introduce a definition for "PAC" (probably approximately correct) coding metrics that substitutes guaranteed minimum guarantees with high-probability bounds.

Although applying Reinforcement Learning (RL) after Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) pre-training is a flexible approach to boost Neural Machine Translation (NMT), recent studies suggest these improvements mostly arise from promoting tokens that were already likely post-pre-training. We propose instead that the vast action space constitutes the primary impediment to RL success in machine translation. To validate this, we performed two series of experiments that support our view. Firstly, shrinking the vocabulary size was shown to enhance the efficacy of RL. Secondly, reducing the action-space dimension while keeping the vocabulary size constant similarly yielded meaningful gains across BLEU scores, semantic similarity metrics, and human judgments. notably, significant performance jumps occurred in RL outcomes and improved translation fluency.

The time-periodic dynamics of open quantum systems attract considerable interest due to their ability to reach a unique, dynamic balance characterized by continuous flow, distinguishing them from an isolated thermal steady state. This specific experimental work investigates the effects of periodic and discrete time driving on a single photon interacting with its environment. We present a robust theoretical modeling that aligns closely with experimental data and provides a key analytical description for these out-of-equilibrium states. Ultimately, it appears that by tuning the driving parameters, we can effectively decide the degree of separation between the resulting dynamic states and pure equilibrium.

We argue that these dimensionless networks represent a distinct hierarchy in network organization, harboring hierarchical structure through shape and size dynamics that remain invisible through conventional analysis methods.

We analyzed 13 days of high-cadence data from the FIELDS instrument on Parker Solar Probe (PSP) to examine how heliospheric wind energy flows as a function of distance from the Sun. Using de-cadence proton junction temperatures recorded near a coronal hole's inner heliospheric stream, we identified three distinct regimes characterized by different scaling laws for proton junction temperature ($T_p$) relative to the heliocentric distance ($r$): power laws with specific exponents for $r < 0.3$ AU (regime A), $0.3$ AU $< r < 04$ AU (regime B), and a unique behavior beyond this range. These findings suggest that inner heliospheric winds evolve through three phases: (i) near-r (Region A), where viscous heating, likely due to magnetic field-line reconnection, dominates; (ii) an intermediate zone (Region B), marked by reduced heating and spatially varying resistance effects. This regime is followed by a transition at $r > 0.4$ AU, leading to a $T_p \sim r$ relationship. This transition marks the shift from the dominant resistive and viscous heating mechanisms to a state of thermal/adiabatic change, ultimately helping explain key features of inner heliospheric thermal structures.

Speech-emotion recognition (SER) empowers computers to interact emotionally intelligently. Although current SER models achieve high accuracy in controlled laboratory settings, they struggle when deployed in actual environments with diverse and changing data domains. Model performance typically drops significantly due to this distribution mismatch, a challenge known as domain adaptation (DA). We propose a strategy that integrates DA and Reinforcement Learning (RL) to enhance SER across domains. This method employs a reference library of domain-specific performance metrics to guide the RL process, enabling the selection of optimal pre-trained emotion classification models for target domains. Furthermore, we introduce an adaptation mechanism to refine these choices further within each new domain, leveraging RL to maximize effectiveness in live applications. Our extensive experiments, spanning four distinct emotional voice types, confirm that this Domain-adaptive Referred RL (DarrL) method not only surpasses standard transfer learning approaches but also delivers substantial performance gains over using static reference libraries for RL.

This study addresses a distributed optimization challenge in multi-agent systems where a subset of nodes behave maliciously. Specifically, these adversaries attempt to drive the network off the optimal trajectory by corrupting data transmitted to their neighbors and imposing high bandwidth costs through excessive communication. Accordingly, we introduce a quantized, distributed gradient-based algorithm designed for benign agents. This section establishes the convergence of the proposed method to a vicinity of the global optimal solution, analytizing performance under both bandwidth constraints and adversarial interference. Detecting fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background (CMB), often called anisotropies, is among the most vital techniques in cosmological research. Due to the faintness of this signal, scientists have needed increasingly sophisticated and sensitive detectors capable of operating in daunting environments like high altitudes, deep polar regions, and aboard satellites. As these detectors grow more sensitive, instrumental systematic errors have become a dominant source of noise alongside cosmic factors. This paper introduces *s4cmb*, a generic forward modeling simulation framework designed to identify such systematics. *s4cmb* translates the physical properties of individual detector elements and the associated biases into prediction errors for measured time-ordered data. This allows researchers to generate large-scale, realistic datasets incorporating both physical and instrumental effects for specific missions. Ultimately, these simulations provide the testbeds needed to validate analysis methods for constraining or eliminating the identified systematic errors.

Word reordering represents a language generation challenge where models must arrange unordered inputs into coherent text using ordered output, based primarily on existing research employing standard models or neural networks. Despite this history, researchers have not yet investigated the benefits of large, word-oriented language models or proposed reasons why pre-trained ones succeed in these scenarios. In our work with the BART model, both its effectiveness in solving word reordering problems and the capacity for BART to generate multiple parallel translations are implemented. Additionally, we conduct analysis on trained prefed translations and syntactic re arrangements to explore how this model operates. Ultimately, we discover that parallel output generation by BART along with its capacity for understanding word re arrangement leads to improved performance in these challenging tasks.

The swift evolution in generating and distributing synthetic media across images and video has created a pressing need for effective detection methods capable of handling the complex patterns introduced by the wide array of synthesis techniques available today. To enhance the accuracy of falsification identification, this study applies classical transform methods in spatial, frequency, and transform domains as feature sources. This synthesized feature set forms the model's input, addressing the limitation that relying on data from a single transform domain often leads to suboptimal performance. Furthermore, we introduce a novel architecture known as MD-CSDNetwork. This design integrates features extracted via Discrete Cosine Transform (DCC), Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT), and Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) at the architecture's initial stages using a cross-stitching mechanism. Consequently, network models gain direct and seamless access to multi-domain feature representations. Additionally, separate sub-networks are trained for each specific transform method, ensuring they do not interfere one another during the learning phase. Our experiments, conducted on the deepfakes face-based fake news dataset and sox multi-forge video dataset, show improvements of up to 4.5% and 3.5% over current state-of-the-art approaches.

As pyramids inherently require massive, unsustainable growth, they require sophisticated mechanisms to recruit continuously until inevitable bankruptcy. Recurrent accusations of a pyramid structure were evident in Forsage's design, yet the creators justified it by comparing their payout model to gambling winnings. Our analysis reveals Forsage was effectively a pyramid scheme concealed behind a gambling narrative.

Thousley, et al. (2016) analyzed archival ultraviolet data to assess how accretion influences the spectral output of AD Leonis during the 1985 April outburst. Using \phoebe\ code simulations, they fit observational data under both radiatively driven and disk-inclined accretion scenarios. The best matches indicate a near-star continuum consistent with disk-inclined accretion occurring near the critical rotation limit, implying an outflow mass flow of ~$10^{-4} \, \text{M}_\odot \text{yr}^{-1}$ (approximately 1000 times the system's baseline). Consequently, the star likely underwent a transition from a low-mass dwarf to an intermediate object classified as an Herbig Ae (HAe) star, rather than remaining low-mass dwarf. Furthermore, the derived high disk inclination (~45°) aligns with the inclination derived from IR polarization studies.

Neural network architectures for point clouds have demonstrated significant success in tasks like classification and detection. However, recent studies indicate that these models are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, which employ various "flattening" methods to transform point data into standard tensor formats, process them through neural networks, and reconstruct the points as images or tabular data. This study proposes a hypothesis: the varying susceptibility of these architectures to attacks is dictated by the specific smoothing transformations used. To validate this, we introduce, compare, and test numerous smoothing techniques across different point cloud task paradigms. Our evaluation includes varying the smoothing parameters and dimensions while also examining their impact on detected object detection. Ultimately, we highlight the established connection between smoothing design and attack efficacy, providing an extensive benchmark that offers in-depth insights into the points of aggregation. This study serves as an foundational resource for evaluating future algorithms and clarifies the geometric characteristics required for robustness against future adversarial data.

The Jost function method has been adapted within the RPA framework to detect poles in complex energy planes, enabling the determination of parameters for RPA interactions used in nuclear calculations. These selected parameters yield accurate results for the electric dipole responses of $^{16}$O. Specifically, a RPA pole identified in the first excited states of this nucleus corresponds to the "giant dipole resonance," characterized by an electric dipole response peak near the 20 million K temperature threshold.

Community detection poses significant challenges yet remains highly relevant across diverse fields, ranging from social and biological domains to physics and power grid infrastructure. However, addressing these issues in dissipative systems present as isolated non-equilibrium states harboring emergent phenomena adds another layer of complexity. This work investigates the formation of structure within isolated but nowhere-equilibrium dissipative systems, utilizing the Hosseinian diagram—a tool popular in the study of electrical grid stability—as the primary method of analysis. It is shown that this framework enables the identification of meta-stable regimes characterised by a group switch phenomenon, where a slight perturbation on a specific subset of nodes precipitates a widespread collapse affecting an extensive region. It is also argued that influences flowing between nodes drive this collective behavior, with the Hossainian diagram serving as a visualization for node grouping based on such connectivity. Such node groupings exhibit the features of a first-order phase change, where an abrupt and sudden shift from one metastable state to another occurs. Such discoveries offer new perspectives on how we understand and categorize stability in the context of power networks. Such findings are notably important for the field of power systems engineering, as understanding these dynamics aids significantly in effectively preventing and managing unwanted and large-scale blackouts.

Implementing neural text generation models via Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) presents significant challenges due to the non-differentiability of the full training loop, a limitation existing approaches address poorly with either inaccurate gradient estimates or poor-quality sentence embeddings. Drawing inspiration from sparse coding, we introduce SparseGAN to feed sparse, semantically meaningful sentence representations to the discriminator. This is achieved by treating the embedding matrix as overcomplete basis vectors and the average token embeddings of sentences as coding signals over this basis. We approximate these bases using k-means clustering, with the resulting cluster centers utilized as input to the generator. To generate sentences, we employ an RNN with an attention mechanism that encodes these cluster centers directly. Furthermore, we address the implementation difficulty of sparse training for a generative adversarial network, ensuring effective collaboration between adversary and generator within this novel framework.

The concept that life can migrate across planetary systems, known as interstellar panspermia, dates back decades but remains hard to validate through observation. To evaluate the chances of confirming this phenomenon, we established a mathematical framework accounting for factors such as the lifespan of resilient microbes in transit, the dispersion of stellar velocities, and the distribution of ejected material. Our results indicate that the statistical pair distribution of inhabited planetary systems can effectively detect interstellar transfer of life under the specific condition that ejecta move with sufficient divergence relative to stellar motions. By offering estimable parameters for these ejecta velocities, we can refine lower-bounds on how widely this interstellar seeding occurs.

A core objective of wildlife research is to estimate population sizes. Within this field, a primary goal involves understanding how animals utilize environmental resources. Spatial capture-recapture (SCR) models address both objectives concurrently by estimating key SCR parameters alongside additional covariate-dependent SCR functions. By integrating standard SCR models with additional information on resource selection, we evaluate three distinct approaches: standard SCR models nested within a full hierarchical Bayesian framework, covariate-dependent SCR functions paired with information-on-selection methods utilizing binary smoothing penalties, and covariate-dependent SCR functions calibrated under the maximum likelihood estimate. Using a simulated case, we demonstrate that all three strategies effectively estimate standard SCR parameters and produce accurate inferences on resource selection. However, estimating the correlation between an individual's capture probability and its location requires hierarchical Bayesian models. Finally, we analyze a real-world data set involving endangered Florida panthers to estimate the study area's central density and to evaluate how individuals select habitats based on fine-scaled locations. Our analysis finds a positive relationship between capture probability and habitat quality, indicating that more highly protected areas are occupied by more abundant cat populations.

Multilayer networks represent a valuable tool for modeling and analyzing the dynamical behaviors of diverse systems. Formal verification techniques have been broadened to incorporate software testing, with the goal of jointly improving program reliability across development, validation, and evolution. Our geometric testing theory serves as a foundation for this testing paradigm, defining a testing problem through a specific geometric structure known as a code space. Within this space, feasible executions are represented as paths connecting points that represent individual variable assignments. We analyze feasibility by treating the system under test along this space as an abstract interpretation, using standard semantics to identify legal paths and a newly defined topology to characterize space features. Our approach leverages the intrinsic geometry to reconcile standard testing strategies, proposing innovations in both theory and application. We introduce a traversal methodology that generates inputs capable of executing syntactically and dynamically feasible paths, while our geometric model also enables progress guarantees, formal continuity conditions, input synthesis for previously unreachable practical outcomes, and detection of bugs associated with semantic inconsistencies. Empirical data indicates that programs evaluated via these techniques achieve a coverage level of 90.6% along compared to 82.5% in standard environments, while demonstrating more complex execution flows with higher cyclic and cyclic ratios relative to prior methods.

We address the fundamental task of counting nodes in a network of unknown dimensions, which is sparsely connected and affected by Byzantine faults, where a significant portion of malicious nodes act arbitrarily to maximize confusion. Our prior work demonstrated that size estimation is feasible in ideal small-world networks, characterized by the rapid spread of walks, even under Byzantine attacks; however, those studies were limited to this specific, optimal network model. In the work presented here, we generalize the setting to three dimensions of network structure: the presence of generalized local similarity, where a large proportion of arbitrary nodes appear similar to the explorer from a proximal perspective; the existence of some expandability, ensuring that not all adversarial nodes appear similar to the explorer; and the dimension of the expando lity structure from the explorer's vantage. We utilize these properties to classify the problem into distinct complexity tiers based on the guaranteed accuracy achievable for estimation. Specifically, we show that if either generalized local similarity or any form of expandability holds, there exists a strategy that size estimates with constant relative error requirements within a polynomial amount of time relative to the square root of the actual network dimension. We provide formal definitions for each structural assumption within the context of explorer operations and identify various small-world phenomena that inherently satisfy these conditions.

Accurate traffic control depends on effectively estimating traffic states. This research proposes an integrative, nonparametric technique for short-term queue length estimation, utilizing partial queue observations on a cycle-by-cycle basis collected from probe vehicles. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on random arrival assumptions or the need for primary parameter calibration, this method employs straightforward algebraic formulations contingent solely on signal timing. Specifically, for a given approach lane, conditional queue lengths are modeled using a Negative Hypergeometric distribution based on probe location, counts, timestamp, and time intervals (such as signal phase termination). Field test data comparing these nonparametric estimators against both parametric models and standard Highway Capacity Manual methods demonstrates that the new technique achieves parity in accuracy when estimating queue lengths.

While brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) effectively promote upper-body recovery in those with spinal cord injuries, their utility for walking support remains limited. A primary limitation is the tendency to lower-dimensional movement spaces of the cervical spinal cord, which necessitates continuous and frequent user attention. Our study aimed to decode step frequency and walking states for free gait in this specific population. Using an electrocorticogram (ECoG) interface implanted for BCIG purposes, we decoded step frequency during natural walking alongside two trained 2D joystick movements: one dedicated signaling entry into walking mode and the other serving quality control. Our data analysis showed that step frequency decoded from high-graphical representations clustered distinctly based on actual gait. Additionally, identified BCIG skill progress—marked by accurate decoding of walking modes and step frequency—correlated strongly with improved control over a high-graphical interface. These outcomes suggest a path toward more immersive and sustained engagement for BCIG users who have sustained spinal cord injuries affecting locomotion.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have proven to be highly effective for handling graph-structured data across diverse fields, including natural language understanding, knowledge reasoning, and natural scene analysis. However, estimating the connectivity from multidimensional time series data—which is prevalent in areas like bio-signal processing, finance, and climate science—remains challenging. Moreover, existing GNN approaches typically assume a static effective connectivity that does not evolve over the dynamic nature of such data. This paper addresses both issues by introducing a dynamic and adaptive graph convolutional network capable of modeling and predicting changes in effective connectivity. Evaluations across synthetic and real-world datasets illustrate the model's superiority in identifying effective connectivity patterns and capturing their temporal fluctuations compared to current methods.

Animals move to achieve various goals, including foraging for food, seeking mates, navigating and colonizing new areas, and evading predators. Although this activity is diverse, almost all animal movement shares the common characteristic of producing visible motion from an external view. Consequently, analyzing video data offers a powerful non-invasive method for studying and understanding animal behavior in natural and controlled environments. However, accurately detecting and reconstructing this movement remains difficult due to inherent challenges such as variable lighting, obstructed views, complex camera movements, and the lack of fixed landmarks. Addressing these issues, we present a robust and general computational model designed specifically for detecting animal locomotion within video footage. By representing an individual frame and its corresponding motion as a superpixel-based sparse code, the model identifies objects moving biologically by applying principles known from neuroscience and biology regarding expected biological motion patterns. Demonstrating the approach's efficacy across several species, including insects, spiders, fish, and mammals, we show a reliable capacity to distinguish organic movement from other types of motion, with significant potential applications in fields such as pest control and zoology.

Known as the Kaczanewski-Davidson (KDY) method, third-order iterative schemes provide an efficient and robust approach for approximate matrix inversion, presenting a compelling alternative to standard numerical libraries when dealing with massive and sparse matrices. This approach traces its origins from the Davisson (Davidson) optimization technique in molecular physics to the Davisson (Davidson)-Householder (DH) strategy for enhancing second-order methods. Building on this foundation, this paper introduces a novel general third-order formulation that subsumes the original YKY and the Davisson (Davidson)-Householder (DH) approaches. Furthermore, the work presents efficient implementations optimized for GPU architectures and derives potential generalizations to even higher orders.

Various physical setups, ranging from ultracold atoms to artificial lattices in solid-state materials, are now capable of investigating topological insulators characterized by complex band structures. A prominent trend in this field involves introducing disorder to these systems to observe the emergence of topologically non-trivial phases induced by it, utilizing disordered analogs of clean systems as platforms. Despite the richness of disorder types available in these advanced architectures, most have focused on fully random randomness. This study introduces a novel, efficient, and computationally accessible topological non-trivial phase within a disordered square-Huckel square-lattice system perturbed by binary randomness. Interestingly, this binary randomness induces a competition between the topologically protected and trivial insulated states within the mobility energy spectrum. The results highlight how binary disorder uniquely influences the movement of topologically protected bands and the positioning of the unknotty localized levels. Consequently, the criteria for topological phase transition are modified and refined, accounting for the specific effects of binary randomness.

This paper investigates the maximum performance improvement achieved by optimal power control compared to binary (on/off) schemes within large interference networks. Leveraging Extremal Network construction and Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) theory, it is demonstrated that for a given binary power-control network achieving a specific GDoF, there exists a corresponding optimally controlled network where the target transmit powers match the binary constraints, such that its GDoF increases by a factor of $\gamma$. Crucially, this ratio satisfies $\gamma \geq \sqrt{K}$ for sufficiently big network sizes $K$. Consequently, binary power control strategies inherently incur significant performance losses, with the extremal multiplicative gap reaching up to $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ in progressively larger interferences systems.

Validated using systems ranging from a single collision event to large scales, this approach effectively integrates multiple time regimes: the detailed dynamics near the moment of impact are captured with a short step ($\Delta t_0$), while broader dynamics are managed efficiently via the MSA step. findings indicate that fluid dynamics are accurately resolved even when the MSA time-step is one hundred times larger than the initial step. Specifically, in a box containing 500 particles, simulation efficiency improved by approximately $4\text{--}5$ times compared to the standard small-time-step method. Locomotion over unpaved grounds is recognized as a pivotal capability for exploratory robotics, with recent advances highlighting legged systems—ranging from quadrupeds to monopods—as particularly promising. A primary obstacle in this domain is the compaction and instability of soft terrain, which dissipates energy and disrupts balance. This study presents a novel elasto-plastic soil model designed to simulate hopping on loose gravel. The model integrates dry friction within a shear-strength failure criterion and derives a tension-dependent stiffness to capture volume change. First, this elasto-plastic framework is validated against existing linear spring models used for rigid-leg robots encountering loose substrate. Second, the integrated terrain physics is applied to a one-degree-of-freedom hopping leg to investigate natural dynamics and generate stable jumping trajectories via optimal control. Although the exact complex physics of granular materials present inherent challenges in trajectory design, successful simulation results under this elasto-plastic conditions demonstrate only minor deviations compared to ideal behavior on firm surfaces. While these results effectively illustrate the terrain mechanics and dynamic challenges, further development is required to achieve viable algorithms suitable for real-world deployment on actual hardware.

Spectroscopic methods rely on the interplay between matter and light to reveal material properties, yet advancing these techniques often requires dealing with complex outputs that are hard to interpret directly. We demonstrate a hybridized mixed finite element method implemented on a new class of discrete fractured-porous domain where fluid can only move along fractures.
